title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 53
paragraphs: Fourth is the river Borysthenes, which is both the largest of these after the Ister and also, in our opinion, the most serviceable, not only of the Scythian rivers but of all the rivers of the world besides, except only the Nile of Egypt—for no other river can be compared with the Nile. Of the rest, however, the Borysthenes is the most serviceable, since it provides the fairest and richest pastures for cattle; and fish which are by far the best and most numerous of any river; and the sweetest water to drink; and it flows with a clear stream, though others beside it are turbid; and along its banks crops grow better than anywhere else, while in parts not sown, grass grows deeper. Moreover, at its mouth salt forms of itself in abundance; and it produces huge spineless fish, which they call antacaioi, used for salting, as well as many other things worthy of wonder. As far as the region of the Gerrians, which is a forty days' voyage, the Borysthenes is known as flowing from the north wind; but beyond this, no one can tell through what nations it flows. It is certain, however, that it runs through desert to the land of the agricultural Scythians, for these Scythians dwell along its banks for a distance of ten days' sail. Of this river alone and of the Nile, I cannot tell where the sources are, nor, I think, can any of the Hellenes. When the Borysthenes comes near the sea in its course, the Hypanis mingles with it, running out into the same marsh; and the space between these two rivers, a kind of beak of land, is called the Point of Hippoles, and in it is placed a temple of the Mother. Opposite the temple, on the river Hypanis, the Borysthenites are settled.
